---
title: "Protocol to result"
---

A trial's result begins as a sentence in a protocol and ends as a number in a table. Between
them sit an analysis plan, a programming specification, several datasets and a succession of
people, each interpreting the last one's work.

Three standards aim to change that. ICH M11 gives the protocol a fixed structure, USDM turns it
into data, and CDISC's Analysis and Derivation Concepts describe how a measurement becomes a
result. Together they aim at a path from that sentence to that number in which **every step is
declared rather than implied**, so that a reviewer reads the declaration instead of a program.

This book teaches that path by walking it. It takes one analysis of a public, simulated
oncology trial from the protocol's sentence to an executed result, and shows every choice on
the way: what is chosen, from which published list, and which sentence in the study's documents
decides it.

## What is declared

The declaration has three parts, and the stages are organised around them:

- a **biomedical concept** says *what is measured* — here, alanine aminotransferase, a liver
  enzyme;
- a **derivation concept** says *how each subject's analysed value is computed* — here, the
  change from that subject's baseline;
- an **analysis concept** says *what result is computed across subjects* — here, the difference
  between the two arms from an ANCOVA.

Together they form a **chain**: a measurement, what is derived from it, and the analysis of
what was derived.

A chain is written as data, not prose, so software can read it and carry it out. Normally a
programmer reads the analysis plan and writes code for that one study. Here a general-purpose
program — the *engine* — takes the chain and the study's dataset and produces the result, and
nobody writes analysis code for the study.

## One estimate, reached two ways

Is the ambition worth the trouble? That depends on what a loosely declared step costs, and the
book's worked example shows one. The question is the change from baseline in alanine
aminotransferase at Cycle 2 Day 1, compared between the two arms. It is answered by two routes,
both starting from the same analysis dataset:

| | Declared route: the chain, run by the engine | Programmed route: the study's own derived variables |
|---|---|---|
| What is measured | Alanine aminotransferase, named by the biomedical concept | The same |
| Which record is baseline | The record at the Baseline visit, as the derivation declares it | The last value on or before the first dose, as the plan defines it. A programmer applied that rule and flagged the record in the dataset |
| The change | Computed by the engine: the value minus that baseline | Read from the dataset, where the programmer computed it |
| The model | ANCOVA, as the analysis concept declares it | The same ANCOVA |
| Treatment difference, placebo minus torivumab | **{{fact:lab.engine.diff|4}}** | **{{fact:lab.reference.diff|4}}** |

The measurement is the same and the model is the same. The two routes part at the derivation,
over which record is a subject's *baseline*.

The plan chooses by date. The chain chooses by visit. These are different rules, because a
subject can have two records at the Baseline visit: a screening draw, and a pre-dose draw on
the first day of treatment. The plan's rule says which of the two counts. The declaration says
only "the Baseline visit", so the engine has nothing to choose with and takes the first record
it finds. For {{fact:lab.baseline.differ}} of {{fact:lab.baseline.subjects}} subjects, the two
rules pick different records.

Nobody chose the visit rule over the plan's. It comes from the published template for change
from baseline, which the chain uses: in the version of the library this book describes, the
template takes its baseline by the visit a record is labelled with, not by its date. The
template leaves the question open, the data makes it matter, and the engine answers it without
saying so.

Both numbers are computed correctly, but only the programmed one follows the plan. Nothing
about the chain showed this: it was complete, and it ran. The plan said which record is
baseline, and the declaration lost that on the way — in one step of the simplest analysis a
trial has.

[Stage 3](stage-3-dc.qmd) is where that declaration is made, and
[stage 7](stage-7-compare.qmd) takes the difference apart.

## Who this is for

Anyone in pharma. No CDISC background is assumed: terms are explained where they first matter,
and linked to their source rather than collected into a glossary you would have to read first.

## Reading it, or running it

**To read this book you do not need to install anything.** Every figure, excerpt and screenshot
is already on the page.

**To run the worked example yourself, set up first.**
[Appendix A — Setting up](setup.qmd) builds everything with one command: the application, the
study and its data. Do it before stage 1, which is where the application first appears. Stages
0 and 0b are about the documents and need nothing installed.

## How it is organised

One chapter per stage: from reading the protocol against a structured template, through the
three kinds of concept, to executing the analysis in the browser and comparing the result with
the datasets a programmer built from the same plan.

Every **stage** chapter answers the same four questions:

- **What this is** — the concept, in plain terms, and where it is published
- **What you do** — the actions, in order, with what was chosen for the worked example and why
- **What you should see** — the expected outcome
- **What to look out for** — the checks worth making before moving on

**This is a book about the concepts, not about the tool.** One application is used throughout:
the eSAP Builder that CDISC publishes alongside the concepts, described in
[the documents chapter](documents.qmd#the-application-used-here). It is there because concepts
you cannot see working are hard to believe and impossible to check, but it is the instrument,
not the subject. So each chapter states the work first, and then how this particular
application does it, under *in the application used here*.

The same distinction applies to the checks. Some are properties of the model and will be true
of any tool. Others are true of this application, in the version this book describes, and may
already have been fixed; those say so. It is worth knowing which is which before you carry a
lesson from this book to a different tool.

**The working record is elsewhere.** How each stage actually went — the false starts, the
workarounds, the decisions taken about this particular study — is kept in the repository behind
the book, and each chapter's *Step into the factory* says where. The chapters keep to what
applies beyond this study.

## Two ways in

Where you join depends on where your protocol came from, and it changes which chapters apply.

| | Stage 0 | Stage 0b | From stage 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Protocol authored to ICH M11** | Confirm the elements your endpoint needs are present and populated | *Does not apply* — nothing to restructure | Identical |
| **Protocol predates M11, or follows a sponsor template** | Map it, element by element, and record what is absent | Move the misplaced content, then regenerate | Identical |

This book walks the second, because the study it uses predates M11 — and because that is the
more common position today. The two converge at stage 1, and everything after it is the same
work either way.

Two later chapters need more than a protocol. **Stage 6 needs analysis datasets** to run
against. **Stage 7 needs a second, independently built implementation** to compare with, which
exists when a study is being re-examined and not when one is being specified for the first
time. Each of those chapters says what to do without it. Stages 0 to 5 need only a protocol and
a set of definitions, and produce a specification whether or not any data exists.

## Two things to know before you start

**The numbers here are read from the runs, not typed.** Every figure is resolved from the
results files at build time, so a figure in this book and the run that produced it cannot
disagree. When the underlying study was regenerated and every number moved, the book moved
with it.

**It does not end in agreement.** The difference between the two estimates above is where the
stages finish, and stage 7 takes it apart rather than smoothing it over.
